refutation.note: Checked at source: studies/rlneurons/results/day1_minp/readout.json (origin/main) gives base_p0.95_T1 409/500, 35 cap hits, 12 rule-A loops against 410, 27, 0 at top-p 1.0. The theory's statement says 'any mode-sharpening truncation (top-p < 1) costs the cued base', and its rival test says top-p 0.95 at T 1.0 'adds about 18 cap hits ... and costs about 12 points'. Measured: +8 cap hits and -1 right. The loop half moved the way the theory says (loops 0 -> 12; min-p 0.1: 0 -> 34 loops, 27 -> 58 cap hits). The accuracy half is flat. Across four sampler settings at T >= 1.0 (top-p 1.0, top-p 0.95, min-p 0.1, T 1.5 + min-p 0.1) the cued base scores 404-412, a 1.6-point band inside the ~3-point GPU-to-GPU noise of knowledge-814454, while cap hits range 27-58. So accuracy is not set by the surprise level the way the statement claims. This is a weak contradiction, not a refutation: 409 and 35 sit inside the theory's own prediction intervals [385, 409] and [33, 65], at their edges, and its refuted_by thresholds (>= 414 right, <= 30 cap hits) were not crossed. Secondary: knowledge-499152 shows the no-answer counts of t09/t10 come from the base's 'Answer:' line format, which grader v1/v2 cannot read (39-46 % of base answers), and not from drift. That is why claim t10 (75 predicted, 127 measured) missed. Read: all 25 after.jsonl items, all 60 before.jsonl items, board ls result knowledge --new --n 30 --full (nothing newer on sampling than result-44b4df), the README section 'Truncation rules at T 1.0' and its readout.json.

wins_judgement: Neither win is specific support for the mechanism. t51 (min-p 0.1 at T 1.0: 404, claim 390 [372, 404], nulls 415/412): the measured change is -1.2 points [-4.6, 2.2], which includes zero and sits inside the ~3-point hardware noise. The claim won only because it guessed a decrease while the nulls guessed an increase. 'Truncation does not change accuracy at T 1.0' predicts about 410 and fits as well. The README does show the 34 new loops fell on 21 problems that were right at min-p 0, so truncation-made loops do cost answers. That supports the loop part, which 2610.24715 and 2512.12895 already predict. But other problems gained (resampling churn), so the net cost is about 6 problems, not the claimed 20. t09 (plain base T 1.0, 166 answers with no extractable answer under v1/v2; claim 130 [95, 170], nulls 45/60): knowledge-499152 explains it more simply. The base ends with an 'Answer:' line that v1/v2 cannot parse in 39-46 % of answers, so 127-166 unreadable answers appear at both temperatures. The theory's 'confusion trap' reading predicted a large T 0.6 vs T 1.0 contrast (75 vs 130). The measurement shows 127 vs 166, and t10 missed. The format account fits both t09 and t10. The theory fits only t09.
rival: The theory's own rival (monotone temperature, additive cue, top-p helps both slightly) loses on loops: truncation at T 1.0 did add loops and cap hits. It ties on accuracy: the cued score held at 409. A simpler rival explains both wins at least as well. It has three parts. (a) At T >= 1.0 the cued base's accuracy is flat in the sampler: truncation brings loops back, but they replace about as many answers as resampling fixes. (b) The no-answer counts are a grader format artefact. (c) The cue's large gain at T 1.0 is the plain base losing coherence on short problems, which the cue prevents; no single surprise optimum is needed. One measurement separates them: the plain base (no cue) on MATH-500 at T 1.0 / top-p 0.95, cap 16,384, grader v3. The theory predicts a rise from 224 to about 262 [240, 290], so the sign of the top-p effect flips between prompts. The flat or monotone rival predicts no rise beyond noise (about 224 +- 15). Supporting check, 15 GPU minutes: the teacher-forced per-token surprise ratio of cued vs plain T 1.0 answers. The theory says 0.6-0.9; a ratio >= 1.0 refutes the 'cue lowers entropy' link.

novelty.nearest: Du et al., 'Optimizing Temperature for Language Models with Multi-Sample Inference' (TURN, 2502.05234): the token-level entropy of a model's generations on a task measures its distance from the task. Lower entropy means a higher optimal temperature (correlation -0.895 on MATH; pretrained base lowest optimum, task-finetuned highest). The loop and truncation half is published as Basu et al. 2007.14966 (boredom and confusion traps; repetition is a near-linear function of cross-entropy, whatever the sampler), Pipis et al. 2512.12895 (risk-averse loops at low T) and 2610.24715 (truncation can lock a loop; pure sampling never locks).
novelty.difference: TURN compares different weights (base vs instruct vs task-finetuned) for majority-vote sampling. It does not treat a 3-token opening cue on fixed weights as the entropy-lowering shift. It also does not predict that tail truncation at T 1.0 has opposite signs for the cued base (loses) and the plain base (gains), and it does not link the cued base's low-T failure to loops that run to the cap.

import_carries_win.which: t51 rests on 2512.12895: its 'why' says min-p cuts the tail at flat positions where progress mass is spread over paraphrases, which is that paper's risk-aversion mechanism. t09 rests on 2007.14966: its 'why' is the confusion trap. Without the imports, t51 is a sign guess inside noise, and t09 follows from the grader format fact in knowledge-499152 with no import at all.

verdict_sentence: No team result refutes it by its own thresholds, but its two wins are explained as well by noise (t51) and by a grader format artefact (t09, which also explains its t10 miss); its loop half is published (2007.14966, 2512.12895, 2610.24715) and its entropy-to-optimal-temperature half is published across models (2502.05234), leaving only the untested prompt-level sign flip of top-p (plain base at T 1.0 / top-p 0.95) as new.
